Nothing fetches a page on a timer; a row is current for `review_days` after it was read and is shown as not recently checked after that. A name the code uses with no row here fails scripts/sources_check.py. W948 (FU-1066): a row that names `hosts` says what its terms, as read, `permits` this platform to do; an empty `permits` means NOT TO BE USED, and the check fails if any of its hosts appears in the code. W1156 (FU-1060): the check reads every .py and .json file under agentic_core/ and every .ts and .tsx file under the app's src/, so a name anywhere in the backend or on any page needs its row.

rows.says: GOV.UK records it as first published 7 October 2016 and last updated 14 September 2026; it is aimed primarily at solicitors and other conveyancers. A legal interest in land cannot be conveyed or created without a deed, with exceptions such as assents and short leases (Law of Property Act 1925 ss.52 and 54(2)); electronic dispositions under the Land Registration Act 2002 s.91 are not covered. A deed must be in writing, make clear on its face that it is intended to be a deed, and be validly executed as one (section 1.2). An individual signs (a mark counts) in the presence of a witness who attests and who is not a party to the deed, and delivers it (section 2.1); the guide cites the Law Commission's 2019 conclusion that 'in the presence of a witness' requires the witness's physical presence. A company executes under its common seal, or by two authorised signatories, or by one director whose signature is witnessed and attested, and a deed is presumed delivered on execution (section 3, citing the Companies Act 2006 ss.44 and 46). Prescribed attestation clauses are given for registered land.
rows.not_read: sections 4 to 16 (unregistered companies, other corporations, overseas companies, local authorities, office-holders in insolvency, charity trustees, powers of attorney and the rest) beyond their headings; practice guide 82 on electronic signatures; the update history

rows.read_by: round W1148, the publisher's own text read whole (its data file at legislation.gov.uk), not through a summary; first entered by a research reader of round W711 through a fetch that summarised the page, whose statement was incomplete
rows.says: In this form from 1 January 2010; no outstanding change is listed on the publisher's record (the file was last modified 31 August 2015). An instrument is not a deed unless it makes clear on its face that it is intended to be one (by describing itself as a deed, being expressed to be executed or signed as one, or otherwise) and is validly executed as a deed; being under seal does not by itself make that clear (s.1(2), (2A)). An individual validly executes an instrument as a deed if, and only if, it is signed by the individual in the presence of a witness who attests the signature, or at the individual's direction and in their presence and the presence of two witnesses who each attest it, and it is delivered as a deed (s.1(3)); making one's mark counts as signing (s.1(4)). Where a relevant lawyer delivers an instrument as a deed for a party, it is conclusively presumed in favour of a purchaser that the lawyer was authorised to (s.1(5)).

rows.says: No outstanding change touches the Schedule on the publisher's record (the file was last modified 8 January 2025). It defines the six reserved legal activities: rights of audience, the conduct of litigation, reserved instrument activities, probate activities, notarial activities and the administration of oaths. Reserved instrument activities are preparing an instrument of transfer or charge for the purposes of the Land Registration Act 2002, making an application or lodging a document for registration under it, and preparing any other instrument relating to real or personal estate for the purposes of the law of England and Wales, or relating to court proceedings there (para.5(1)). An instrument includes a contract for the sale or other disposition of land, except a contract to grant a short lease (Law of Property Act 1925 s.54(2)), and excludes a will, an agreement not intended to be executed as a deed, a letter or power of attorney, and a transfer of stock with no trust or limitation (para.5(3), (4)). Section 14 (in this form from 7 February 2023) makes carrying on a reserved legal activity when not entitled an offence, with a defence of not knowing and not reasonably being expected to know.

rows.read_by: round W1148, the publisher's own text read whole (its data file at legislation.gov.uk), not through a summary, with sections 43 and 46
rows.says: In this form from 6 April 2008; no outstanding change touches it on the publisher's record (the Act's file was last modified 24 July 2026). Under the law of England and Wales or Northern Ireland a company executes a document by affixing its common seal, or by signature: by two authorised signatories (every director, and the secretary of a private company that has one or of a public company), or by a director in the presence of a witness who attests the signature (s.44(1) to (3)). Signed so and expressed to be executed by the company, it has the same effect as under seal (s.44(4)); in favour of a purchaser in good faith for valuable consideration it is deemed duly executed if it purports to be signed so (s.44(5)); one person signing for more than one company signs separately in each capacity (s.44(6)). Read with it: a contract is made by the company under its seal, or on its behalf by a person acting under its authority, express or implied (s.43); a document is validly executed by a company as a deed if, and only if, it is duly executed and delivered as a deed, delivery being presumed on execution unless a contrary intention is proved (s.46).
rows.not_read: the Scottish rule (s.48) and the rest of Part 4; any company's own articles, which may say more about who signs

rows.read_by: round W1148, the publisher's own text read whole (its data file at legislation.gov.uk), not through a summary: sections 61 to 76 and Schedule 2
rows.says: In force from 1 October 2015 (s.73 in this form from 31 December 2020, s.74 from 1 January 2024); no outstanding change touches Part 2 on the publisher's record. It applies to a contract between a trader and a consumer, and to a consumer notice (s.61). An unfair term or notice is not binding on the consumer, who may still rely on it; a term is unfair if, contrary to the requirement of good faith, it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations to the detriment of the consumer, judged by its subject matter and all the circumstances when it was agreed (s.62). Schedule 2 Part 1 is an indicative and non-exhaustive list of twenty kinds of term that may be unfair (s.63). The main subject matter and the appropriateness of the price are excluded from the assessment only if the term is transparent and prominent (s.64). A trader cannot exclude or restrict liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence (s.65). A written term must be transparent (s.68); a term that could have different meanings takes the one most favourable to the consumer (s.69); a court must consider fairness of its own motion where it has the material (s.71).
rows.not_read: Part 1 (goods, digital content and services) and its exclusion rules in ss.31, 47 and 57; Schedules 3 and 5 (enforcement); the CMA's guidance on unfair terms

rows.read_by: round W1148, the publisher's own text read whole (its data file at legislation.gov.uk), not through a summary: Part I, sections 1 to 14, and Schedule 2
rows.says: No outstanding change is listed on the publisher's record (the file was last modified 17 May 2024); since 1 October 2016 Part I no longer covers consumer contracts, which the Consumer Rights Act 2015 covers. Sections 2 to 7 apply only to business liability. Liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence cannot be excluded or restricted, and other loss from negligence only so far as the term or notice satisfies the requirement of reasonableness (s.2). Where one party deals on the other's written standard terms of business, the other cannot exclude liability for its own breach, or claim to render a substantially different performance or none, except so far as reasonable (s.3). The seller's obligations as to title cannot be excluded, and those as to description, quality and fitness only so far as reasonable (s.6; s.7 for other contracts under which goods pass). The requirement of reasonableness is that the term was a fair and reasonable one to include, given what the parties knew or ought reasonably to have known when the contract was made, and it is for the party relying on it to show that it was (s.11); Schedule 2 lists guidelines, among them the parties' relative bargaining strength and whether the customer knew or ought reasonably to have known of the term.

names: Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998
rows.read_by: round W1148, the publisher's own text read whole (its data file at legislation.gov.uk), not through a summary: regulations 1 to 12
rows.says: In force from 5 December 1998 (regs 2, 9 and 11 in their present form from 31 December 2020); no outstanding change is listed on the publisher's record (the file was last modified 16 May 2024). The duties fall on an employer for lifting equipment provided for or used by its employees at work, on a self-employed person, and on a person who has control, to the extent of that control, of lifting equipment, of a person at work who uses it, or of the way it is used, in connection with a business or other undertaking; not on a person who supplies it by sale or hire-purchase (reg.3). Lifting equipment must be of adequate strength and stability (reg.4), safe for lifting persons (reg.5), positioned to reduce risk as low as is reasonably practicable (reg.6) and marked with its safe working loads (reg.7); every lifting operation is planned by a competent person, supervised and carried out safely (reg.8). It is thoroughly examined before first use, after installation, and, where exposed to deterioration, at least every 6 months (equipment for lifting persons, and accessories) or every 12 months (other equipment), or under an examination scheme, and after exceptional circumstances (reg.9). A defect is notified forthwith and reported in writing, and the equipment is not used until it is rectified (reg.10); reports and records are kept for set periods (reg.11).

'Check if you can make a claim': there is a different way to make a claim to an employment tribunal in Northern Ireland, linked at https://www.employmenttribunalsni.co.uk/how-make-claim; a person usually has 6 months if the problem happened on or after 1 October 2026, and 3 months if before; to find the deadline for a claim, check the employment tribunal time limits guidance on the Acas website, linked at https://www.acas.org.uk/employment-tribunal-time-limits; a person may not be able to claim if the deadline is missed, even while trying to resolve the dispute directly; interim relief is applied for within 7 days of dismissal. rows.says: Shown as last updated 16 November 2026. The law on time limits changed on 1 October 2026. Before it, 3 months minus 1 day for most claims and 6 months minus 1 day for a few (statutory redundancy pay, equal pay, certain claims against a trade union, certain armed forces claims): its worked example, paid the wrong amount on 30 September 2026, ends at 11:59pm on 29 December 2026. On or after it, 6 months minus 1 day for most claims: its worked example, 1 October 2026, ends at 11:59pm on 31 March 2027. In Scotland the limit for breach of contract claims changed on 9 November 2026. The first step is to notify Acas, within the limit; early conciliation pauses the limit only if Acas is notified within it; grievance and appeal procedures do not change it; interim relief has a 7-day limit; a claim out of time may still be made, and the judge decides whether to accept it, though limits are in most cases strictly enforced.

names: How to make a claim (the Industrial Tribunals and the Fair Employment Tribunal, Northern Ireland)
rows.read_by: round W1162, the page's own text read whole at its site, not through a summary
rows.says: Most tribunal claims must be made within three months of the incident, though this varies, is subject to early conciliation, and claims usually have to be presented within three or six months depending on the type of claim; the tribunals extend a limit only in exceptional circumstances, and a claim made out of time may not be heard. The tribunals give no advice. From 27 January 2020 most claimants must first notify the Labour Relations Agency and consider early conciliation, which allows up to a calendar month, and two weeks more if needed, without affecting the deadline.
